# Summary

For half a century the UK's official statisticians have published regular
projections of how long we can expect to live. Plotting every vintage of
those projections against what actually happened tells a clear,
three-act story:

1. **Under-projection (to ~2010).** Successive projections repeatedly
   *underestimated* how fast life expectancy would rise. Each new round had
   to be revised upward. Simple linear extrapolation of past gains would
   have beaten the official forecasts --- the phenomenon @white2002longevity
   and @oeppen2002broken drew attention to, and which led @lee2019mortality
   to accept that directly extrapolating life expectancy is often adequate.
2. **Over-projection (2010--2019).** Improvement stalled. The rounds from
   2008--2016 kept projecting the old rate of gain and now sit well *above*
   what was observed --- the forecasters were, for the first time in the
   series, systematically too optimistic.
3. **Shock and pessimism (2020--2024).** The pandemic produced a sharp drop
   in 2020, and the 2020-, 2022- and 2024-based rounds are dramatically more
   pessimistic than anything before them --- even as 2022--2024 show a
   partial recovery.

The single figure below is the whole argument.

# The figure

```{r}
#| label: fig-fan
#| fig-cap: "ONS life expectancy projection rounds, 1971 to 2024 (coloured, dark = older rounds), against actual estimates (black). Each coloured line is one projection vintage extrapolating forward from its base year."
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(
  here::here("bayes_paper", "figures", "M02_ons_lt_projns_updated.png")
)
```

The figure is produced by `scripts/update_ons_projections_figure.R`, which
combines the ONS National Population Projections accuracy-report underlying
data (1971--2012 rounds) [@ons_npp_accuracy] with the biennial *expectation
of life, principal projection* datasets (2014--2024 rounds)
[@ons_expectation_of_life], overlaid on actual period life expectancy at
birth.

# The numbers behind the story

Mean annual gain in UK period life expectancy at birth (years):

| Era | Female | Male |
|---|---|---|
| 1991--2010 | 0.19 | 0.28 |
| 2011--2019 | 0.10 | 0.12 |
| 2020--2024 | 0.01 | −0.02 |

The 2010s roughly halved the pre-2010 rate of improvement; the pandemic
half-decade erased it almost entirely, though the sign of the 2020--2024
average is dominated by the single large 2020 fall (UK: −0.88 years for
females, −1.20 for males) and masks renewed gains in 2022--2024.

# Why this deserves to stand alone

Three reasons this figure is more than a supporting exhibit:

- **It is legible without statistics.** The under- then over-projection
  reversal is visible at a glance; no model is needed to see it.
- **It reframes a live policy question.** "Are the official projections
  believable?" has a different answer in each act. The most recent rounds
  have swung to pessimism precisely when the underlying data are most
  ambiguous (a genuine stall, or a pandemic interruption followed by
  recovery?).
- **It is a natural teaching case** in forecast evaluation: five decades of
  a single institution's forecasts, scoreable against outturn, is rare.

# Caveats

- The final actual point (2024) is the projection base year and is
  part-estimated.
- Pre-2019 actuals use ONS single-year life tables
  [@ons_single_year_lifetables]; 2019--2024 use the historic estimates
  embedded in the 2024-based projection file, which differ from the older
  series by up to ~0.17 years for Wales (population rebasing after the 2021
  census).
- "Actual" period life expectancy is itself a synthetic period measure, not
  a cohort's realised lifespan.
